what_its_for: Anastrozole is used to treat breast cancer in women who have gone through menopause. It works by lowering the amount of estrogen your body makes, which can slow down or stop the growth of certain types of breast cancer cells that need estrogen to grow. It may also be used to help prevent breast cancer from coming back.
how_to_take: Take anastrozole by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day so it becomes part of your routine. Do not crush or chew the tablet.
dosing: The usual dose is one 1 mg tablet taken once a day. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly. Do not take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is not too close to the time of your next scheduled dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store anastrozole at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicines down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about proper disposal.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking estrogen-containing products (such as hormone replacement therapy, estrogen pills, patches, or creams) while taking anastrozole, as they can make this medicine less effective. Avoid tamoxifen, as it should not be taken at the same time as anastrozole. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before starting any new medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements, especially St. John's Wort or DHEA. Alcohol may increase the risk of bone loss, so try to limit or avoid it.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: chest pain or shortness of breath (possible signs of a blood clot or heart problem); sudden severe headache, vision changes, or weakness on one side of the body (possible signs of a stroke); severe bone, joint, or muscle pain; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or trouble breathing; unusual vaginal bleeding; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; or symptoms of severe depression or unusual mood changes. Also let your doctor know about any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Anastrozole starts working right away to lower estrogen levels in your body. However, it may take several weeks to months before you or your doctor can see the full benefit on your cancer. It is very important to keep taking this medicine every day as prescribed, even if you feel well. Most women take anastrozole for at least 5 years as recommended by their doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Anastrozole must NOT be used if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant must use effective non-hormonal birth control during treatment. Bone health: Because anastrozole lowers estrogen, it can weaken your bones over time and increase the risk of osteoporosis and fractures. Your doctor may recommend calcium and vitamin D supplements and regular bone density tests. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, as your doctor may need to monitor you more closely. Older adults: No special dose adjustment is usually needed for older adults.
